extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; critics and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation of Joseph Addison's essays, Spectator series, dramas, and public conduct — identifying qualities of style, characterization, invention, moderation, and professional behaviour that make his work exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent, believable narrator/persona
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator himself was conceived and drawn by Addison; ... a gentleman who, after passing a studious youth ... has travelled ... has bestowed much attention on curious points of antiquity ... an insurmountable bashfulness prevents him from opening his mouth, except in a small circle of intimate friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a distinct, consistent observing persona with believable background, habits, and social limits; the persona's limitations (e.g., bashfulness) may shape voice and what is reported rather than narrated directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop rough sketches into vivid characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Four of the club ... were uninteresting figures, fit only for a background. But the other two, an old country baronet and an old town rake ... had some good strokes. Addison took the rude outlines into his own hands, retouched them, coloured them, and is in truth the creator of the Sir Roger de Coverley and the Will Honeycomb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with simple outlines for secondary figures but retouch and enrich them into memorable, humanized characters; small good strokes can be elaborated into enduring portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series structure: unity through recurring narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Every valuable essay in the series may be read with pleasure separately; yet the five or six hundred essays form a whole, and a whole which has the interest of a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design serial essays so each can stand alone while contributing to a larger, connective narrative (recurring characters, events) that gives cumulative interest similar to a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ordinary events to create narrative unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The events were such events as occur every day. Sir Roger comes up to town ... goes with the Spectator on the water ... walks among the tombs ... is frightened by the Mohawks ... the Spectator pays a visit ... hears a point of law ... at last a letter ... brings ... news that Sir Roger is dead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bind a series together through truthful, everyday incidents rather than contrived plots; realistic small events can produce sustained reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose virtues: truth, grace, wit, humour, pathos, and insight
rubrics_metrics.description: They are related with such truth, such grace, such wit, such humour, such pathos, such knowledge of the human heart, such knowledge of the ways of the world, that they charm us on the hundredth perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for writing that combines truthful observation, elegant expression, comic and pathetic touch, and psychological/worldly understanding — qualities that reward repeated readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unflagging invention and avoidance of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: His invention never seems to flag; nor is he ever under the necessity of repeating himself, or of wearing out a subject. There are no dregs in his wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain freshness across many pieces by varying approach and material; avoid rehashing the same jokes or themes until they become stale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate variety of forms and moods
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Monday we have an allegory ... on the Tuesday an Eastern apologue ... on the Wednesday, a character ... on the Thursday, a scene from common life ... on the Friday, some sly Horatian pleasantry ... on the Saturday a religious meditation ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a regular variety of genres and tones (allegory, apologue, character-sketch, domestic scene, satirical pleasantry, religious meditation) across a series to sustain interest and showcase range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select representative samples to judge range
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who wishes to form a just notion of the extent and variety of Addison’s powers, will do well to read at one sitting the following papers ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an author's range, consult a curated set of representative pieces (serious, comic, allegory, character, narrative) rather than isolated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical writing should be luminous and ingenious (but audience-aware)
rubrics_metrics.description: The least valuable of Addison’s contributions to the Spectator are, in the judgment of our age, his critical papers. Yet his critical papers are always luminous, and often ingenious. ... The best of them were much too good for his readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for clear, ingenious criticism, but be mindful of audience readiness; criticism that is technically excellent may be underappreciated if it exceeds contemporary taste or expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain moderation and humanity in political/polemic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Among his political works the Freeholder is entitled to the first place. ... It is difficult to extol too highly the candour and humanity of a political writer whom even the excitement of civil war cannot hurry into unseemly violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in partisan writing, favor measured argument, clemency, and respect for opponents rather than invective; moral authority is enhanced by moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid calumny; use ridicule without cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison, who calumniated and insulted nobody, ... gifted with incomparable powers of ridicule, he had never even in self-defence, used those powers inhumanly or uncourteously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ satire and ridicule to expose folly, but refrain from personal calumny or uncourteous attacks; humane ridicule preserves the writer's dignity and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official and administrative prose should be simple and unpretending
rubrics_metrics.description: It was well observed ... that Addison never, in any official document, affected wit or eloquence, and that his despatches are, without exception, remarkable for unpretending simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal or governmental documents favour plain, straightforward expression over rhetorical flourish; clarity and decorum are paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic quality for neo-classical tragedy: dialogue and declamation
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare it with the masterpieces of the Attic stage ... would be absurd ... Yet it contains excellent dialogue and declamation, and among plays fashioned on the French model, must be allowed to rank high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragedies in the French/neo-classical model emphasize strong, declamatory speeches and polished dialogue even if not matching ancient Greek grandeur; judge plays within their stylistic school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional fairness toward rivals and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: We hope ... no man in Addison’s situation could have acted more fairly and kindly, both towards Pope and towards Tickell, than he appears to have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fairness in professional relations: avoid conspiratorial behaviour, extend credit where due, be open about assistance and corrections, and resist petty rivalries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer not to recast a successful imaginative work
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule undoubtedly is that, when a successful work of imagination has been produced, it should not be recast. ... All these attempts failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about extensively revising or expanding a successful imaginative piece; the original balance that pleased readers can be spoiled by heavy-handed recasting.
